Text: The first time I ever heard the Crickets, I was hooked. Their harmonies, just the sheer atmosphere they created. I wanted desperately to be able to make music like that.
Context: On discovering Buddy Holly and the Crickets as a boy

Text: I would listen to the songs and want to know everything - how the harmonies worked, why they worked, what made one harmony affect you in a certain way.
Context: On dissecting records as a teenager

Text: He collected anything! He had collections of Eagle comics, cheese labels, puzzles and matchbox tops - amongst other things!
Context: Brian's mother, recalling his childhood collecting habit

Text: Those lessons took place at the back of our German class. I used to tape a paper fingerboard to my wrist, to simulate a guitar neck. Needless to say, Brian went on to pass his German O level, I didn't!
Context: Schoolfriend, on Brian teaching him guitar

Text: We used to set up two tape recorders - I would play lead guitar, not too well I might add, into one, and Brian would play the chords. Then we would play back those two tracks, and over them Brian would play my cheap and nasty home-made bass guitar, and I would hit anything within reach - hat boxes and the like - as drums.
Context: On early home recording sessions with Brian

Text: We all wore stuff that looked like army uniforms - we wanted a regimented look for some reason. It was such a small gig too, but we were so confident. We went down pretty well.
Context: On 1984's first gig, St Mary's Church Hall, 28 October 1964

Text: All our gear broke down one night. The audience were getting restless, so I played a non-stop, half-hour drum solo to fill the gap until the equipment was fixed. I earned an extra ten bob for that!
Context: 1984's drummer, on a gig going wrong

Text: Wow, his fingers look blurred they're going so fast!
Context: Reacting to Brian playing a fast guitar passage at the Molesey Boat Club (later revealed the record had been sped up in mixing)

Text: It was like a scene out of a Wild West movie. There were bottles flying and chairs being smashed over people's heads. But the band played on!
Context: Describing a fight breaking out at a White Hart gig in Southall

Text: Which way's the stage, man?
Context: Passing 1984 as they tried to sneak out to watch his set at Imperial College, 1967

Text: And I won a Barbra Streisand album.
Context: On the prize for 1984 winning a talent contest at the Top Rank Club, Croydon

Text: We were so proud of him. We knew that his music was so very important to him, but we secretly hoped he would continue studying, and finish his thesis. He'd done so much work towards it. But we were prepared to stand by him whatever he chose.
Context: Brian's mother, on his graduation day at the Royal Albert Hall

Text: None of us could actually play. We just stood there and strummed and twanged tuneless chords, it was dreadful! But we invited the neighbours and some friends along, and we charged them to get in!
Context: On his first band, the Bubblingover Boys

Text: Roger was so ambitious, and his confidence in himself was immense. He just knew that one day he would make a name for himself and be living in London. I knew it too in my heart.
Context: Roger's mother, recalling his teenage ambition

Text: I was a lazy scholar, I hated studying and I was certainly given no privileges.
Context: On his school days at Truro School

Text: I remember the first time I saw Roger on drums. His flamboyance just blew me away.
Context: On first seeing Roger Taylor play, at their audition meeting

Text: I loathed cricket, and long-distance running, I was completely useless at both! But I could sprint, I was good at hockey, and I was just brilliant in the boxing ring, believe it or not!
Context: Recalling his school sports at St Peter's

Text: Freddie was excellent at all sports, but when I heard about the boxing, I wrote to him from Zanzibar, where we were living, and told him to stop that, I didn't like the idea, it was too violent.
Context: Freddie's mother

Text: In Zanzibar, at that time, the native people would make and sell handicrafts, ornaments and lots of local hand-made things. Freddie was strolling in the park one day when a local boy passed with his wares, and Freddie fell in love with a little ornament of a deer and her fawn.
Context: Recounting a childhood story about Freddie's generosity

Text: I asked him why, and he said he needed to lend a friend some money, as he was being thrown out of his flat and desperately needed it. I thought it would be ten pounds or so. He asked for fifty pounds! ... That was his way, always generous, always thoughtful of others.
Context: On teenage Freddie giving away his savings

Text: Ibex were going nowhere fast. They had so much talent though, and it didn't go unnoticed by Freddie. He was a kind, penniless, outrageous guy, and he loved Ibex.
Context: Ibex's roadie/manager, on the band Freddie joined in 1969

Text: We auditioned Freddie to take over lead vocals from Mike. It was at Imperial College. We were all competent players... but none of us was particularly good at singing. Freddie had a great voice, with a terrific range, but he didn't really know how to use it.
Context: Ibex's drummer, on auditioning Freddie

Text: We just used to yell at him, 'For goodness' sake, Freddie, just stand still!' He was all over the place, such energy, but it wasn't done then!
Context: Ibex guitarist, on Freddie's flamboyant early stage moves

Text: Most mornings Freddie would be up first. He had a white Fender Telecaster and he would walk around the flat, stepping over the various bodies still trying to get some sleep, strumming and singing the Who's 'Tommy'. He knew every chord and all the words. It was quite a ritual.
Context: On Freddie's morning routine in the Ferry Road flat

Text: I've never seen anyone write songs quite like Freddie. He would start singing and strumming the guitar, and then someone would have to sit by him and write down what he sang. I never once saw him write anything down, someone else always did. It was spontaneous, but it made sense.
Context: On Freddie's songwriting process

Text: We had a party one night. Tupp made these cakes, with dope in them. I refused to touch them, but everyone else had some. Then at about midnight the police came... We invited them in, and gave them a drink and a couple of these cakes. We all fell about, but they left, not knowing a thing.
Context: Recalling a Liverpool flat party

Text: I felt like such an outsider when I first joined the band. They had everything worked out. Just before my first gig, Freddie suggested we all camp it up and wear women's clothes. He really wanted to play on it, but it just didn't happen, thank God!
Context: On joining Queen as bassist in 1970

Text: I was getting tired of playing. I wanted to try other things, get what everyone called a 'proper job', and I missed Cornwall. I thought, even then, that this band might one day make it big. But that didn't stop me wanting to get out.
Context: Queen's first bassist, on leaving the band

Text: On one occasion they were all there, all the bands, and they were playing so loudly. It was way past midnight. The next day we were thrown out, evicted! But it was such a fun time, we all laughed so much. We were all so thin too, we didn't have very much money, although what we had we all shared.
Context: On the shared Sinclair Road flat scene in the Ibex/Smile days

Text: They were all dressed in black, and the lights were very dim too, so all I could really see were four shadowy figures. They didn't make a lasting impression on me at the time.
Context: On first seeing Queen play, before he joined the band

Text: We thought he was great. We were all so used to each other, and were so over the top, we thought that because he was quiet he would fit in with us without too much upheaval. He was a great bass player too - and the fact that he was a wizard with electronics was definitely a deciding factor!
Context: On the band's decision to recruit John Deacon

Text: We all sat there, and then this huge pair of tits came on screen. That was it, we were in fits, crying with laughter. We couldn't stop. Eventually, the manager came up and threw us out. That made us giggle all the more as we staggered up the aisle to the exit!
Context: Recalling an ill-advised cinema trip on tour

Text: Suddenly we could all smell burning. It was dreadful, an awful smell. My Dad was the first to realise that it was Brian's boots - they were melting!
Context: On Brian warming his feet too close to the fire while staying with her family

Text: He jumped up and down in a manner most incongruous.
Context: On short-lived bassist Doug's over-the-top stage antics before he was fired

Text: I'll call you soon...
Context: Producer, after watching Queen play Imperial College with their new line-up, 11 July 1971

Text: That night we saw such an improvement. They were brilliant; they were happier with each other, they were well rehearsed. It just came across to us, and we felt that we were witnessing the emergence of a band of star status.
Context: Freddie's dressmaker friend, on a 1970 Queen gig

Text: I was in a position to give them work. I knew talent when I saw it, and they had it in abundance, all they needed was a break.
Context: On booking early Queen gigs on Merseyside

Text: They were very fussy. The songs were done one by one. They would carry on until they thought it was right. It sometimes took a very long time. But they put up with so much shit too, during that time.
Context: Producer/engineer at De Lane Lea studios, on early Queen sessions

Text: I had heard Wreckage play this track in a rehearsal, and particularly liked one riff, but the rest of the song was changed drastically by the four of us, using some of my own riffs and Freddie's words.
Context: On the origins of the song 'Liar'

Text: As far as I'm concerned the person who wrote the words has effectively written the song.
Context: On the band's early songwriting-credit rule

Text: It took Freddie nearly six months to finally ask me out! I thought he fancied my best friend, so I used to avoid him. One night we were at one of his gigs, and after it had finished he came looking for me. I left him at the bar with my friend to go to the loo, but I actually sneaked out. He was furious!
Context: On how she and Freddie got together

Text: There was never a doubt, darling, never. I just knew we would make it, and I told everyone who asked just that.
Context: On Queen's prospects at the end of 1971, still largely unknown

Text: I found that first tape interesting. You could tell there was talent individually, and they could play, they were good musicians. But I was wary of making a full commitment at such an early stage.
Context: Trident boss, on first hearing Queen's demo tape

Text: I heard that Queen sound, and I just knew it had promise, how could I not? I knew that John Anthony had a good ear for talent, and this was yet more proof of that.
Context: Queen's early manager, on first hearing the demo tape

Text: They all told me that Queen just weren't going to happen. They were crazy. But I had to find someone who was qualified - we had an investment in Queen, and their careers.
Context: On the difficulty of finding Queen a manager

Text: No, no, no. I've got a group called Humble Pie who are going to be much bigger than this group will ever be.
Context: American manager, declining to take on Queen, 1972

Text: It took me over a year to get Queen a deal, and everyone turned them down, I mean everyone. I won't name names as some of those people turned out to be my best friends and I don't want to tarnish their reputations! But they know who they are, every one of them.
Context: On the long struggle to land Queen a record deal

Text: I had been played hundreds of tapes that week, from people's mothers to their howling dogs and by bands and artists interested in the new label. None of them grabbed me, I was bored! Then Ronnie Beck handed me this Queen tape, and I listened. I was knocked out.
Context: EMI executive, on discovering Queen's demo at the 1973 MIDEM festival

Text: Queen had by now played Liverpool so many times that we had a following there. Amongst them were some fans who had taken up our black and white theme, and gone so far as to paint their fingernails alternately black and white. One night after a show they produced their nail varnish bottle, and amidst much drinking, painted Freddie's nails black and mine white.
Context: On the origin of the black-and-white nail-varnish look

Text: Freddie spent a whole hour in front of the mirror in the bedroom, just choosing which belt to wear! He would come out in each one and ask our opinion. We just wanted to go out! He was so vain, but we tolerated it, everyone did. It was part of him, part of his character. He just wouldn't have been Freddie without that vanity.
Context: Close friend, on Freddie's fastidious sense of style

Text: Oh, they were full of ideas. They knew how they wanted to look, how they wanted to be represented, how they wanted to be packaged. They just came in to see me, plonked a stack of photos on the desk and said, 'These are what you can use, and this is our logo.' My job from then on wasn't too difficult.
Context: Queen's early publicist, on the band's clear creative vision

Text: It went somewhat against the grain, and perhaps triggered a growing sense of where my life ought to be going.
Context: On working an EMI Electronics job assessing fragmentation-bomb damage while Queen was taking off

Text: Their following was really strong, even then. We'd have grandparents turning up with their children and their grandchildren, it was amazing!
Context: Trident boss, on Queen's early live following

Text: It was all so exciting. It was such a big place, and we had only ever seen him play at little halls before. We were probably the oldest ones there, and as we were taking our seats a young fan came over and asked us who's mum and dad we were. When we told him he asked us for our autographs. It was a wonderful show.
Context: Brian's mother, on seeing Queen play Hammersmith Odeon for the first time

Text: A great relationship had already grown between the bands off stage. We learned a lot about stagecraft and back-stage organisation from Mott and their entourage - as well as having enormous - and outrageous - fun!
Context: On touring as support to Mott the Hoople

Text: Hold it! Do you want more Queen?... Do you want more of those Pommy bastards?... Or do you want a good old Aussie band?... How about Madden Lake?
Context: Manipulating the Sunbury Festival crowd out of demanding a Queen encore, 1974

Text: One Tuesday evening I was working late in my Manchester Square office... The windows were wide open and I had the Queen white label on, again! ... As I was about to leave, the phone rang. It was Robin Nash, the producer of BBC's Top Of The Pops. They had a last-minute space in that Thursday's show, and did I know anyone? I said yes.
Context: EMI promotions chief, on how Queen landed their first Top of the Pops slot

Text: The day after Top Of The Pops, Steve Harley from Cockney Rebel came storming into my office. He was furious, he slammed his fists on the desk and told me all I cared about was Queen, what about his band? I just looked him in the eye, and said, 'It's your turn on the Pops next week.' I hadn't a clue! I was just trying to placate the man. But believe it or not, by sheer fluke, Cockney Rebel were on the following week.
Context: On placating a rival band's furious frontman

Text: It was Jack. He said he'd had Freddie on the phone, who, after listening to the white label test pressing, said it was the wrong mix and that there was no way that mix could be played on the radio.
Context: On Freddie's insistence on correcting the mix of 'Seven Seas Of Rhye' at the last minute

Text: Freddie was just being so pedantic, so Brian told him he was an old tart. He got really upset and stormed off... When it came to the soundcheck we couldn't find him anywhere, so they turned up the volume on the mike and Brian started yelling 'Freddiepoos, where are you?' He was livid, but it worked and he came flouncing back in, and the band just got on with it.
Context: On a backstage row before the Rainbow Theatre show, 1974

Text: They were great. A real 'sex, drugs and rock and roll' band, we knew we were going to have a great tour!
Context: On touring America with Mott the Hoople in 1974

Text: I introduced myself to him, and we just sat down together and decided we really didn't give a damn who went on first. Jo brought out a bottle of Jack Daniel's whisky and we proceeded to get really, really 'relaxed'. We were so drunk we could hardly walk by the time the argument finished. We've been friends ever since!
Context: On meeting Aerosmith's Joe Perry backstage in Harrisburg, 1974

Text: When we finally went on, I remember, through a haze, whacking the first chord and realising that, among the echo, I couldn't hear a thing. I played the whole show from memory, and decided to compensate by giving it lots of action. Everyone thought it was wonderful! So I decided two things for the future: (1) I would always 'give it action' and (2) I would never drink more than a pint before a show. I have since stuck by both of those resolutions.
Context: On the drunken Harrisburg gig with Aerosmith

Text: The first morning I woke up in the Parker House in Boston, I felt like my whole body was made of lead. I tried to eat a grapefruit... then I dragged myself to the bathroom mirror, and saw that I was a deep shade of yellow. That was the end of our dream of conquering America at one shake. I felt I had let everyone down.
Context: On discovering he had hepatitis mid-tour, 1974

Text: When I finally got out of hospital there was, of course, a mountain of playing to catch up on, plus the vocal harmony parts that needed the depth of the three voices... 'Now I'm Here' was started and finished in the last couple of weeks, since I'd finally got my ideas straight for the song while in hospital, reflecting on the Mott tour and the future.
Context: On finishing Sheer Heart Attack after his hospital stay

Text: It was amazing. All these little Japanese people screaming and yelling for us. We couldn't take it all in, it was like another world, but we loved it!
Context: On Queen's reception arriving in Tokyo in 1975

Text: We were in a hotel in Southampton, we were there for a gig or something, as the band were all staying in the same place, and I had popped out. When I came back I bumped into John Deacon in the lobby, and he said they were number one. I was really pleased, and Roger was excited, but it didn't really sink in. Then, on the way home in the car, they played the song on the radio, saying it was Britain's number one. I suddenly realised that my son was a huge success, he really had made it. It was quite emotional.
Context: Roger's mother, on learning 'Bohemian Rhapsody' hit UK number one

Text: Apart from having to be a Freddie-clone for a while, my other job was to pull all the thorns off the dozens of red roses that Freddie would later throw out into the audience. They wanted to be sure that no one in the audience was hurt, but really it was Freddie who was worried about getting thorns in his fingers.
Context: Queen's personal assistant, on his role in the 'Now I'm Here' stage bit and rose duty

Text: We spent plenty of time catching up on gossip and tour news, and we all ended up singing backing vocals on one of the tracks, called 'You Nearly Did Me In', which also featured the late great bass player Jaco Pastorius.
Context: On visiting Ian Hunter's New York recording session, 1976

Text: Promoter Howard Rose put me in touch with Queen when they were looking for a tour manager for the States. I didn't have a clue who they were!
Context: On becoming Queen's tour manager, 1976

Text: The police threatened to arrest Freddie if he tried to go back out on stage, as he was furious at having no chance for an encore and was going to go back on and give the crowd what they were yelling for. But the thought of being in jail in tights didn't appeal to him at all, so he gave up!
Context: Tour manager, on the aftermath of the Hyde Park free concert, 1976

Text: The intro featured multi-tracked guitars climbing a 'never ending staircase' a la Mr Escher. 'Tie Your Mother Down' became the stage opener at that point. It was actually written with this in mind.
Context: Explaining the Escher-inspired guitar intro used to open the 1977 European tour

Text: I have always wanted to swing from a chandelier. And when I saw this exquisite cut-crystal thing dangling there I just could not resist it!
Context: On swinging from a chandelier at Roger's birthday party in Montreux

Text: If you'd stood under it you'd know why.
Context: Explaining why the band's 1978 lighting rig was nicknamed 'The Pizza Oven'

Text: It was just dreadful. It was bright, nauseating green. But it was too late to do anything about it, I just had to go on stage with it like that. It was so embarrassing and Freddie took the piss all night.
Context: On accidentally bleaching his hair green before a huge German festival show, 1979

Text: Throw it in the lake, dear, what do you think?
Context: Asked by engineer David Richards what Queen intended to do with newly-purchased Mountain Studios

Text: Who are the Queens?
Context: Film producer, on first hearing Queen's name before commissioning them for the Flash Gordon soundtrack

Text: Oh, fucking hell, are you lot here again?
Context: Nightly greeting to the same group of fans (nicknamed 'the Royal Family') at the front row in Paris, 1979

Text: We had played the big places, and although we loved them, and felt it was good that more and more people could come and see us, we also felt we were losing touch with the audience. Our whole show was about audience contact - we felt close to them, they felt close to us. But with those big places they were so far away, so distant. So we got Gerry Stickells to find some small, silly venues for us.
Context: Explaining the idea behind the 1979 'Crazy Tour'

Text: The doctors told me to take it easy for a while. But none of them have ever been on the road with Queen. That advice is almost impossible to take. The tour might have been small in venue size, but it was a hassle. Some of the places were just so tiny that trying to cram in a band the size of Queen was nigh on impossible. But that's what they pay me for, working miracles. So we did it.
Context: On returning to work after collapsing from exhaustion during the Crazy Tour

Text: We wanted to experiment with all that new studio equipment. We had always been keen to try out anything new or different whilst recording. The synthesisers then were so good, they were very advanced compared to the early Moogs, which did little more than make a series of weird noises. The ones we were using could duplicate all sorts of sounds and instruments - you could get a whole orchestra out of them at the touch of a button. Amazing.
Context: On Queen's decision to finally use synthesisers on The Game

Text: 'Another One Bites The Dust' was never an easy song to pull off on stage - the drums didn't have the 'snap' of the record, and some audiences evidently found it 'not very rock and roll'. But we persevered, feeling it was an important song - Freddie especially felt this. What happened independently was that the song was picked up by a major black radio station in New York City, apparently they thought we were a black act.
Context: On the surprise crossover success of 'Another One Bites The Dust'

Text: I'd had these ideas for years, and I just thought the time was right to start putting them into some sort of order. I'd had a go with the single, but I had an album full of songs that I knew couldn't be done by Queen. I don't really know why they were not suitable for us as a band, they just weren't.
Context: On beginning work on his debut solo album

Text: It was my fault. I forgot the chords and got to the chorus too soon.
Context: On a stumble during Queen's emotional live tribute to John Lennon, December 1980

Text: There was no one at all in South America who had the experience to promote anything as huge as a Queen tour, so I personally flew down to Rio, and set up a temporary production office at the Rio Sheraton Hotel for three months. From there I could easily commute to Buenos Aires to keep an eye on the proceedings.
Context: Queen's business manager, on organising the unprecedented 1981 South American tour

Text: I noticed the equipment they were providing us with had, in every case, always belonged to someone else. We were using huge, Super Trouper spotlights, and they all had Earth, Wind and Fire stencilled on the side. Some other piece of equipment had another band's name on too. It just dawned on me that they had obviously 'confiscated' this gear during previous tours.
Context: On suspicious rental equipment supplied for the 1981 Brazil shows

Text: I was standing with an interpreter, and managed to discover that the chap had, in fact, announced that Ethancourt had died. He said there would be a two-minute silence. But none of the band could understand any of this, and I couldn't go and explain as the TV cameras were still filming. They just stood there, looking nonplussed.
Context: On a chaotic live Venezuelan TV appearance during the 1981 tour, as news of the president's death broke and was retracted on air

Text: Munich had a huge effect on all our lives. Because we spent so much time there, it became almost another home, and a place in which we lived different lives... In retrospect it's probably true to say that our efficiency in Munich was not very good. Our social habits made us generally start work late in the day, feeling tired, and (for me especially, and perhaps for Freddie) the emotional distractions became destructive.
Context: Reflecting on Queen's Munich recording years and their toll

Text: I was terrified. I don't like flying in anything smaller than a jumbo jet, darling, and this thing was so small! But I was told we had photographers and the like at the other end waiting for us to arrive, so I couldn't possibly let them see how shaken I was! My knuckles were white from gripping the arm rests.
Context: On his first-ever helicopter flight, to Milton Keynes, 1982

Text: None of us thought it was a very good gig at the time, we were wishing they had filmed Leeds. I particularly found it hard to get the sound right, and couldn't hear the monitors very well. But Tyne Tees filmed it, and mixed it themselves, with no help from us; and we now think it's one of the better videos of our live shows.
Context: On the surprisingly good Milton Keynes concert film, despite a rough night on stage

Text: Boston had been one of the first American cities to really break for us. They were all so enthusiastic, they had parades and Queen events, it was just great, they loved us.
Context: On Boston's official 'Queen Day' in 1982

Text: We went into the studios for this album with the definite agreement among ourselves that it would not be delivered to Elektra Records. Freddie, in particular, was adamant that to do so would be throwing it away, since he felt the company no longer seemed capable of doing their job. However, we also realised that to buy our way out of the existing deal was going to be expensive, and John, particularly, felt that it may be a huge waste of money. While we recorded, Jim was delegated to sort it out. In the event, we paid $1 million to get out.
Context: On Queen's costly split from Elektra Records to sign with Capitol

Text: In spite of an enthusiastic start with the new company, The Works did, if anything, worse than Hot Space overall in the USA. But this has to be balanced against the fact that Freddie was so depressed about the Elektra situation, it was doubtful if he ever would have agreed to make the album at all.
Context: Reflecting on the making and reception of The Works

Text: We had done some really serious, epic videos in the past, and we just thought it was time we had some fun. We wanted people to know that we didn't take ourselves too seriously, that we could still laugh at ourselves. I think we proved that.
Context: On the outrageous, controversial 'I Want To Break Free' video

Text: We had heard so much about South Africa, about the troubles there, but we had also heard a lot about Sun City, and we wanted to go and see it all for ourselves.
Context: Explaining Queen's controversial decision to play Sun City in 1984

Text: It was quite amazing. The whole atmosphere, the warmth, the great friendliness of the people. You could feel it, it was almost a tangible thing. It was a night I will never forget. I promised those people that one day, Queen would go back to Soweto and play the stadium for them.
Context: On presenting awards in Soweto during the 1984 South Africa tour

Text: I told them we believed that we achieved more in the fight against apartheid by going, and insisting on mixed audiences, than by staying away; that we had been able and willing to have our anti-apartheid views printed in the South African press [unusual at that time]... Finally, I upheld our belief that music should transcend all barriers, unfettered by race or politics.
Context: Defending Queen's Sun City visit to the Musicians' Union General Committee

Text: Not another band who want to close the show.
Context: Live Aid promoter, reacting to Jim Beach's request to discuss Queen's time slot, expecting another headline demand

Text: I did try and point out it wasn't one of his better ideas. Especially as he wouldn't have a clue what a pound coin looked like, so how on earth was he going to make sure the people paid the right price and were given the correct change?
Context: Freddie's personal assistant, on Freddie's impulsive plan to sell ice creams at the Time musical

Text: I bought the whole lot, so I wouldn't have to charge anyone anything.
Context: Explaining his solution to not knowing how to make change while selling ice creams

Text: He was hurling ice lollies and tubs and Cornettos all over the place. They were landing in people's laps, on their heads, it was chaos. Some people even threw them back!
Context: On Freddie's ice-cream-throwing antics at the Dominion Theatre

Text: All the bands involved have paid a lot of attention to their stagecraft and the delivery to the audience. They were all really good.
Context: Judging the Rock School talent competition, 1986

Text: I've got a couple of things here dear, would you like to hear them or not?
Context: Playing early song ideas for Montserrat Caballe at their first meeting in Barcelona, 1987

Text: Oh, why not dear?
Context: Agreeing, with feigned nonchalance, to record a full album with Montserrat Caballe after she suggested it

Text: I've done it. I have captured her voice, on my tape.
Context: After completing the first finished track for the Barcelona album with Montserrat Caballe

Text: What else is there left for me to do?
Context: On completing the Barcelona album exactly as he had envisioned it

Text: Shopping with Freddie is like hitting yourself on the head repeatedly with an ice pick. It feels so good when you stop.
Context: Freddie's personal assistant, on a shopping trip in Japan

Text: Queen couldn't even get arrested in the States right now.
Context: On the band's diminished popularity in America by 1986

Text: A highlight for me was working with Joe Cocker. His presence seemed to infuse the 'scratch band' with an amazing energy. And I was able to play alongside Clapton in 'A Little Help From My Friends'. A thrill!
Context: On performing at the Prince's Trust Gala Concert, 1988

Text: Better by about seven light years than Jason Donovan.
Context: Comparing 'Breakthru' favourably to contemporary pop chart rivals

Text: I don't want to tour any more. I really don't.
Context: In a rare full-band TV interview, on his changed feelings about touring, May 1989

Text: It brought back some great memories. I had seen them perform this song many times with Ariel Bender while we were on tour with them. I particularly remember the night they played it in Memphis. It was a really great feeling, doing it with them after so much had happened to all of us.
Context: On sitting in with Ian Hunter and Mick Ronson at Hammersmith Odeon, early 1990
